observations.quote: THE Admonitory Preface OF OSWALD CROLLIE, Physitian
observations.note: The heading names the writing an Admonitory Preface, gives its author as Oswald Crollie, Physitian, and addresses it to Prince Christian Anhaltin.

observations.quote: COURTEOUS READER
observations.note: The salutation (and OPEN.3, Friendly Reader) speaks to the reader, while the heading addresses the preface to the Prince. The lines given do not explain the two addressees.

observations.quote: the Romans extolled Angerona, and the Grecians admired Hapocrotes for their silence
observations.note: The preface opens with two names praised for silence: silence about secrets is set up as the received norm the author goes on to depart from. The lines given say no more of who the two are.

observations.name: ancient Philosophers
observations.quote: all the ancient Philosophers, by the example of Actaeon, have strictly forbidden to prophane the Secrets, and rashly to prostitute the Treasures of Nature to unworthy and filthy minded men
observations.note: A ban on making the Secrets and Treasures of Nature known to the unworthy is given to the ancient Philosophers, with Actaeon as their example. The author reports it under ALTHOUGH and goes on, with Notwithstanding, to act otherwise.

observations.quote: rashly to prostitute the Treasures of Nature to unworthy and filthy minded men
observations.note: What the ancient Philosophers forbid is giving the Treasures of Nature to the unworthy: by their rule the secrets are meant for some readers only.

observations.quote: our Heavenly Father who is that Sun which richly preventeth us all with his gifts
observations.note: Stated: the Sun here is the Heavenly Father; the text itself says so. Margin note N001 names scripture places at these words.

observations.quote: for he communicateth his light, without respect or envy, to the good and bad, to the thankfull and unkind
observations.note: God gives his light to good and bad alike; this is the ground the author gives for sharing. The words stand beside margin note N001.

observations.quote: We are bound to immitate him whose Children we ought to be
observations.note: Against the rule of silence, the author holds that men are bound to imitate the Father's open giving: his ground for publishing.

observations.quote: recovered from the dark Labyrinth and Circumference of toyle and error, to the plain and clear path and Centre of Rest and Truth
observations.note: Paired figures stated by the text: Labyrinth and Circumference stand with toyle and error, path and Centre with Rest and Truth. Those so brought back are said to be bound most of all to imitate God.

observations.quote: I thought it not good by a kind of inhumane ill will, any longer to hide as in a Napkin, the Talent committed to me by the Father of Lights, by an impious silence
observations.note: The author says he has kept hidden what was committed to him and will hide it no longer; he calls further silence impious.

observations.quote: the Gates of Wisdome ought alwayes to stand open to ingenious men
observations.note: Wisdom should stand open, but the words name ingenious men as those it stands open to.

observations.quote: though the doores of the Muses have never been unlockt, but envy hath indeavoured to shut them again
observations.note: The author says envy has always tried to shut again what was opened.

observations.quote: It is, doubtlesse, a most civil and humane Office, willingly to instruct and guide our erring neighbor
observations.note: Instructing the erring neighbour is called a civil and humane duty.

observations.name: Psal. 145.9. Mat. 5. Luke 19. John 1.5.
observations.quote: Psal. 145.9. Mat. 5. Luke 19. John 1.5
observations.note: The margin names four places of scripture beside the words on the Heavenly Father as Sun shining on all alike.

observations.name: Strabe
observations.quote: men imitate God, when they do good
observations.note: The margin gives a saying on imitating God by doing good and names Strabe, beside the duty to imitate God. A letter in the note is illegible.

observations.name: Victor
observations.quote: The gifts of God grow, & are improved by communicating
observations.note: The margin gives a saying that God's gifts grow by being shared and names Victor.

observations.quote: whose Instrument or pen, at least, in the publishing hereof, I both desire, and hope to be
observations.note: The author presents himself as the instrument or pen of the Divine Majesty in publishing this.

observations.quote: for the profit and advantage of my neighbor in the study and profession of Chymistry
observations.note: A second aim beside God's praise: the profit of his neighbour in Chymistry.

observations.quote: I doe here out of the most deep secret of my heart, set before thee two of the most excellent Spagyrik Mysteries
observations.what: two of the most excellent Spagyrik Mysteries
observations.note: The text announces what it sets before the reader as two things under one name, brought out of the deep secret of the author's heart, that is, till now withheld. The lines given do not say what the two are.

observations.quote: whose preparations, after the mistakes of expence, time and labour, have all of them been first proved by my own handy experience
observations.note: The author says every preparation of the two Mysteries was first proved by his own hands.

observations.quote: which neither by report nor ancient Records, I could yet understand that they have together and at once been published unto this very day
observations.note: As far as he could learn, the two have never before been published together.

observations.quote: It hath ever been far from me to overcharge the Reader with trifles and falshoods
observations.note: He does not load the reader with trifles and falsehoods, of which he calls his age fruitful.

observations.quote: much lesse to fill up a huge Volume with the copies of large Receipts (though I have many lying by me, which with great labour and paines I have got together)
observations.note: He refuses to fill the book with many Receipts, though he says he holds many which he does not print here.

observations.quote: with which hodg-podg-Physitians are already so intangled and overwhelmed
observations.note: The author's judgement of physicians who work from many Receipts.

observations.quote: Some of these have beene prepared by others for the Emperor Rudolph to whom I voluntarily imparted them
observations.note: The margin says the author gave some of these to the Emperor Rudolph of his own will and that others prepared them for him.

observations.quote: The greatest Receipts the greatest Deceits for the most part
observations.note: The margin beside the words on Receipts: the largest receipts are for the most part deceits.

observations.quote: for the space of almost twenty years, in many troubles and painfull peregrinations of various fortune through France, Italy, Germany, Hungary, Poland, Bohemia
observations.note: What he offers was gathered over almost twenty years of travel through six named countries.

observations.quote: I have obtained from men of greatest learning and experience in Chymistry, partly by intreaty, partly by purchase and permutation
observations.note: Much of what he offers came from other men, by asking, buying and exchange.

observations.name: Plin in Epist. ad Vesp.
observations.quote: It is a Civil thing, and full of ingenious modesty, to acknowledge by whom we gained any thing
observations.voice: QUOTED: Plin in Epist. ad Vesp.
observations.note: The margin gives a saying on acknowledging from whom one gained anything and names a writing beside it; it stands beside the account of his sources.

observations.quote: those things, being not a few, which by the blessing of God upon my endeavours, I have found out in the practice of Physick
observations.note: A further part is of his own finding in practice, of which he says he will say nothing.

observations.quote: preferring the publick good before my own private advantage, being moved also by Charity, Christian compassion, and the necessity of sick people
observations.note: The author's stated motives for publishing.

observations.quote: I would first take my eyes in my hand, as I may so say, and by the help of Vulcan search and diligently examine the chief and choycest things
observations.note: The words 'as I may so say' mark the phrase as a figure. He examined the choicest things by the help of Vulcan before commending them to public use. This paragraph does not say what Vulcan is; Interpreted (A's inference): OPEN.4 speaks of Nature's Vulcan and OPEN.5 of the Art of Fire and the triall of fire, which suggests Vulcan here stands for fire.

observations.quote: the Children of knowledge, those searchers out and lovers of Truth
observations.note: The text glosses the Children of knowledge as searchers out and lovers of Truth: those who are to gain cheaply what cost the author dear.

observations.quote: not fallacious opinions (as hitherto in such a deale of Legerdemain they have complained of) but the truth it self so long desired
observations.note: He gives not fallacious opinions, called Legerdemain, but truth found by many experiments.

observations.quote: many things after the revolution of the Platonick year have been returned gratis, and with usury to their owners, whole and entire, and far more compleat
observations.note: He gave things back to those he had them from, more complete than he received them. The lines given do not say what the Platonick year is.

observations.quote: those things which they bragged of as great secrets, seemed to me either common, or so faulty and defective
observations.note: Many secrets he travelled for proved common or faulty.

observations.quote: the imperfection of their many descriptions, was to be made up by me, being all reduced into one onely, and that same first proved by my own Chymicall triall
observations.note: His method: many faulty descriptions are made good, brought into a single one, and that one tried by his own chymical trial.

observations.name: common Chymicall custome
observations.quote: according to that common Chymicall custome, Give something, and take something
observations.note: A saying given as the common custom of exchange among chymists.

observations.quote: in our Conference they got an Egg for a Nut, which when I had crackt with long and fruitlesse paines, I found at last nothing but a worm-eaten kernel
observations.note: A figure for the exchanges: he gave the better thing and got something that proved empty after long work.

observations.name: Poets
observations.quote: Nature's Vulcan, which the Poets commend as the most true Inventer and Teacher of Arts Mysteries
observations.note: The praise of Vulcan as inventor and teacher of the mysteries of art is given to the Poets. The text calls it Nature's Vulcan.

observations.quote: who have written in our time of the more secret Spagyrical preparations from other mens relation & not their own handy experience
observations.note: Most writers of his time on these preparations wrote from what others told them, not their own trial; students, after great cost in vain, lay their lost labour and time to those writers.

observations.quote: by the help of Pyrotechnye, or the Art of Fire and Chymistry
observations.note: The text glosses Pyrotechnye as the Art of Fire and Chymistry.

observations.quote: as many things are spoken of which are never done, so many things fall out between the Theory and the Practice
observations.note: Much is said that is never done; practice departs from theory.

observations.quote: in this study no man is further to be believed, then as every one findeth by his own proper experience, handling and seeing by the due approved triall of fire
observations.note: The author's rule of belief: no one is to be believed beyond what each finds by his own trial of fire.

observations.quote: the due approved triall of fire, which discerneth and separateth that which is false, from that which is true
observations.note: The text says what the trial of fire does: it parts false from true.

observations.quote: Learn by other mens warnings to beware
observations.note: The margin urges learning from others' warnings. Two letters in the note are illegible.

observations.name: Aeschylus
observations.quote: Not he that knowes many things, but he that knowes those things that are most profitable, is to be accounted a wise man
observations.note: A saying given to Aeschylus, used as ground for offering few things. A margin note in a script not transcribed (N008) stands at the head of the paragraph.

observations.quote: I had rather present but few things which are rare and choice
observations.note: The author chooses to give few things, rare and choice.

observations.name: Damascen
observations.quote: Let thy Medicines be few, whose vertue and operations thou hast often tryed
observations.note: A saying given to Damascen: few Medicines, often tried.

observations.quote: there doth not lye hid any more choyce and efficacious, then these chief secrets of the more hidden Medicines here offered
observations.note: He affirms that nothing more choice or effective lies hid in Nature than the secrets offered here, with one exception.

observations.quote: except only that universall and most famous Medicine which the most ancient wise Philosophers had from the beginning of the world
observations.what: that universall and most famous Medicine
observations.note: One Medicine is set apart from and above what is offered: the one the most ancient wise Philosophers had from the beginning of the world.

observations.quote: have extoll'd it as a miracle to their just and lawfull Heirs
observations.note: The universal Medicine was praised by the ancient Philosophers to their just and lawful Heirs: knowledge meant for some.

observations.quote: See Anaxagoras in his Book
observations.note: The margin sends the reader to a book of Anaxagoras beside the words on the riches of Nature; its title is in a script not transcribed. The words beside it are the author's own affirmation (I dare confidently affirm), so the note refers rather than gives them to Anaxagoras.

observations.quote: for that which is good is not alway to be found in that which is great, but that which is great in that which is good
observations.note: A maxim of good over great, given as ground for offering few things.

observations.quote: shall sincerely and as he ought come to the inner rooms of Nature by a holy assiduitie of preparations, joining thereto a diligent contemplation of naturall causes
observations.note: Figure of entering Nature's inner rooms; the way named is steady work at preparations joined with contemplation of natural causes.

observations.quote: if the grace of the most high favour be infused into him
observations.note: Success is made conditional on grace given from above.

observations.quote: bring forth far greater things out of this open bosome of Nature, than they seem to promise at the first sight
observations.note: Nature is called an open bosom: more is to be brought out by the worker's own hands than appears at first sight.

observations.quote: The fruit and great gaine will over and above recompeuce the labour & paines of the Artist
observations.note: The margin promises that the gain will more than repay the Artist's labour.

observations.quote: I have proved but some of those virtues and operations which are assigned to every one in order
observations.note: Here he has himself proved only some of the virtues and operations assigned to each Medicine; OPEN.3 says the preparations have all of them been first proved by his own handy experience. OPEN.3 speaks of preparations, this place of virtues and operations.

observations.quote: as I have set down and shewed their preparations in the work it self
observations.note: The preface points to the work itself as the place where the preparations are set down.

observations.quote: because in the use of Phisick I have found the chiefest part true
observations.note: His ground for trusting the rest: in practice he found the chief part true.

observations.quote: the Spagyriks, or those who know how to discern between true and false, who are well grown and exercised in Chymicall employments
observations.note: The text says who the Spagyriks are: those who can tell true from false and are practised in chymical work.

observations.quote: I mean the Sons of Art, who know the tearms and bounds thereof, and have bathed themselves in the springs of true Philosophy
observations.note: The text says whom it means by the Sons of Art: those who know the terms and bounds of the Art.

observations.quote: who can even by a glance and sight only make a good construction and easily guesse of these things
observations.note: The work is addressed to experts who can construe these things at a glance: meant for some readers.

observations.quote: these preparations doe require such an Artist, and not one of a froward and sottish disposition
observations.note: The preparations are said to need a certain kind of Artist and not another.

observations.quote: who have nothing to doe with the common rabble of Alchymists
observations.note: The Artists he means are set apart from the common rabble of Alchymists.

observations.name: that unworthy reproach and slander
observations.quote: The errors of the Artists are imputed to the Art
observations.note: A reproach the author reports and calls a slander, given as the reason the Sons of Art keep apart from the rabble; the lines given do not name who utters it.

observations.quote: He that misseth his end for want of wit, let him thank his own ignorance, & not lay the fault on Nature, or me
observations.note: The margin lays failure to the worker's own ignorance, not to Nature or the author.

observations.quote: other operations also which have been proved by the long practice and certain experiments of most expert Chymists and now published in one work
observations.note: The operations he has not proved himself rest on the trials of expert Chymists and are published together with the rest in one work.

observations.quote: will satisfie the desire and earnest expectation, by an undoubted performance of the desired effect
observations.note: Here operations proved by other Chymists are said to perform without doubt; OPEN.5 says no man is to be believed further than each finds by his own experience. OPEN.7 addresses this assurance to the Artists who can judge at a glance.

observations.quote: the true and more profound Phisitians, who have been Divinely inspired, moved with a Samaritan-compassion toward their sick neighbors
observations.what: the true and more profound Phisitians
observations.note: The text names the physicians it has in view to use these Medicines, and how they are marked.

observations.quote: who in the fear of God also shall use these Medicines rightly prepared by their own labour, in a convenient and artificiall method
observations.note: The Medicines are to be prepared by the physician's own labour and used with method.

observations.quote: not trusting (unlesse they would be succeslesse) as many doe, to the Sophistical and fraudulent preparations of others
observations.note: A warning against relying on preparations made by others, called Sophistical and fraudulent.

observations.quote: they will know by experience far greater efficacies and operations by the cures they doe, then I can or ought to set down and assign
observations.note: The Medicines do more than he can or ought to set down; the rest is left to the user's experience. The limit on what is written rests on the word ought.

observations.quote: especially if they be administred according to the nature of the diseased, and with the approbation of a Phisitian present
observations.note: How the Medicines are to be given: fitted to the patient and approved by a physician present.

observations.quote: all which by Gods help Truth the daughter of time, will make manifest
observations.note: Proof is left to time: Truth, called the daughter of time, will make it manifest.

observations.quote: But to what danger doe I now expose my self by this publick service?
observations.note: Publishing puts him in danger; he calls it a public service.

observations.quote: I shall oppose all with the buckler of my sincerity and earnest endeavour of deserving well
observations.note: Figure: his sincerity as a shield against critics.

observations.quote: the fore-seen darts of the adversary, to wit, anger, evill speaking, envie, scornfull contempt, the truest testimony of ignorance
observations.note: The text says what the darts are: anger, evil speaking, envy, scornful contempt, called the truest testimony of ignorance.

observations.quote: Ignorance is the inseparable companion of pride and mischief
observations.note: The margin beside the words on carping Criticks ties ignorance to pride and mischief.

observations.quote: The Mysticall Hermetick Philosophers who heretofore in part have pryed into these excellent secrets, will rise against me
observations.note: Numbered 1: the first group he expects to rise against him; they have in part looked into these secrets before.

observations.name: Mysticall Hermetick Philosophers
observations.quote: which with greatest industry and long spent time have been found out and hitherto concealed in deep silence; should so soon be brought to light, and made common to every one
observations.note: Their expected complaint: things found with great industry and kept in deep silence are made common. The words report their complaint, not his own view.

observations.quote: They will accuse me for breaking open the seale of Chymistry
observations.note: The charge he puts in their mouth: Chymistry is sealed, and publishing is breaking the seal.

observations.quote: the close Pytha{G007: 1 letter illegible}orean silence
observations.note: A silence the accusers will say the author was never taught; one letter of the name is illegible. A margin note in a script not transcribed (N014) stands here.

observations.name: Hippocrates
observations.quote: the Rule of Hippocrates, which is, To impart sacred things to sacred persons
observations.note: A rule given to Hippocrates, which the accusers will say the author forgot: sacred things for sacred persons only.

observations.quote: brought the truth of Chymistry, till this time held captive in the prison of shadowes and envy, freely communicating it to posterity
observations.note: Within the charge he reports: the truth of Chymistry is said to have been held captive in shadows and envy until now and to be freely given to posterity by him.

observations.quote: these are the heires of true wisedome, Citizens of the Philosophicall Kingdome, alwayes lovers of God and their neighbor, without envy, or at least ought so to be
observations.note: His answer to these Philosophers: as heirs of true wisdom they are, or ought to be, without envy.

observations.quote: in the true Cabala, Magick and Woarchadumie, there are laid up far better Treasures
observations.note: Three things are named together in which far better Treasures than those published here are laid up: what he publishes is less than what is stored there. The lines given do not say what any of the three is.

observations.quote: A word I doe not understand
observations.note: A margin note at the mark after 'far better Treasures' says a word is not understood. The note does not name the word, and the lines given do not show who speaks in it.

observations.quote: with the help of the Oratory and Laboratory, I mean by asking, seeking, and knocking with unwearied paines and watchfullnesse
observations.note: The text says what it means by Oratory and Laboratory: asking, seeking and knocking with unwearied pains.

observations.quote: which Treasures are to be manifest indifferently to all in due time by the light of Grace and Nature
observations.note: The better Treasures are not yet manifest; they are to be made manifest to all alike in due time. Margin note N016 stands at these words.

observations.quote: after the Bloody Judgement of the Son is first finished, which undoubtedly will follow the Watry (Judgement) of the Father, then in the third Age of the Holy Spirit
observations.what: the third Age of the Holy Spirit
observations.term: third Age of the Holy Spirit
observations.note: Three in order: a Watry Judgement of the Father, a Bloody Judgement of the Son, and a third Age of the Holy Spirit, in which the Treasures are to be manifest.

observations.quote: who to make that manifest which was hid, is wont to renew by fire
observations.note: Said of the Holy Spirit: what was hid is made manifest by a renewing by fire.

observations.quote: Elias the Artist
observations.note: One named as coming in the third Age who, in the words after the margin mark, is to restore all things. Margin note N017 stands at the name.

observations.name: Eccl. 43.33.
observations.quote: Eccl. 43.33
observations.note: The margin names a place of scripture beside the words on Treasures made manifest by the light of Grace and Nature.

observations.name: Zeph. 3.9. Mal. 4.5, 6. Zech 14.9. Ecclesiasticus 48.1,
observations.quote: Zeph. 3.9. Mal. 4.5, 6. Zech 14.9. Ecclesiasticus 48.1
observations.note: The margin names four places of scripture beside the name Elias the Artist.

observations.quote: For every person of the Divinity hath his own proper and appointed Age, ministry or dispensation, as may plainly be gathered out of the twelve Articles of the Apostles Creed, divided into three parts
observations.note: Each person of the Divinity has his own Age; he draws this from the Apostles Creed divided in three. No words of the Creed are given.

observations.quote: so many houres of the great and One Day, viz. The continuance of this world
observations.note: The text says what the great and One Day is: the continuance of this world; the three parts answer to its hours.

observations.quote: And thus they wil not with me begrudge these present crums to our thankfull posterity
observations.note: What he publishes now is called crums, set beside the far better Treasures laid up elsewhere.

observations.quote: these present crums
observations.note: Here what is published is called crums beside far better Treasures; OPEN.6 says nothing more choice and efficacious lies hid in Nature than the secrets here offered, the universal Medicine alone excepted. The lines given do not say whether the better Treasures are that Medicine.

observations.quote: who by the light of Nature shall be skillfull in the Chymicks, and stirred up of God to the preparation hereof
observations.note: The posterity the publication is meant for: those skilled by the light of Nature and stirred up by God to prepare these things.

observations.quote: these Chymicall secrets will never be finger'd by those sluggish, slothfull, or sottish despisers of them, by reason of their indisposition and unfitnesse to manuall operation
observations.note: The secrets guard themselves: the slothful will never reach them, being unfit for work with the hands.

observations.quote: there will be little danger of their apprehending and discerning these Divine revealed Mysteries, which are mingled together in a fit place
observations.note: The unworthy are unlikely to grasp the Mysteries, which are said to be 'mingled together in a fit place'. Interpreted (A's reading): the contents are arranged so that unworthy readers miss them. The lines given do not say which place or how they are mingled.

observations.quote: are not quick of understanding in these things which the wise-hearted can apprehend in few words
observations.note: Few words suffice for the wise-hearted; the profane lack the understanding for them: brevity meant for some readers.

observations.quote: these Chymicall secrets will never be finger'd by those sluggish, slothfull, or sottish despisers of them
observations.note: Here, and in N018 (only the worthy shall understand), the secrets stay out of reach of the unfit and unworthy; OPEN.2 gives as the pattern to imitate a Father who gives his light to good and bad alike. OPEN.2 speaks of giving, this place of who will grasp.

observations.quote: Only they that are worthy shall understand these things, viz. They whose humane reason God hath inlightned by the mind
observations.note: The margin says only the worthy shall understand, and says who they are: those whose human reason God has enlightened by the mind.

observations.quote: Let none therefore judge rashly, passing sentence before he know the truth of the cause
observations.note: The margin warns against judging before knowing the matter.

observations.quote: As for the spurious and adulterous Theophrasteans (the worst and wickedest sort of men)
observations.note: Numbered 2: the second group he expects against him.

observations.quote: they will not forbear to accuse my fincerity with all outragiousnesse
observations.note: He expects this group to attack him with outrage.

observations.quote: they may not carry their cheating impostures up and downe the Country to put them off by their feigned experience, counterfeit friendship, disguised piety, various and vain promises at a great rate
observations.note: Why they will be angry: the publication stops them selling impostures dearly under feigned experience and piety.

observations.quote: hunt after a name of learning, wisedome, and prudence among great men, concealing their Authors
observations.note: Some pick up sentences from others and seek a name by them while hiding whom they had them from; set against N006 on acknowledging sources.

observations.quote: their forged Cachochymicall and Sophisticall Arts, which have not so much as a spark of truth in them
observations.note: His name and judgement for the false arts this group sells, set apart from true chymistry.

observations.quote: their Pharisaicall skin which hideth the Fox-like and cursed mind would be pluckt off
observations.note: Figure: an outward skin hiding the true mind, which they fear publication will strip off.

observations.quote: are wont not only falsly to accuse many innocent men of upright, vertuous and blamelesse life, but also to bring their honest and commendable name into hatred and hazard
observations.note: These Impostors falsely accuse blameless men and endanger their good name.

observations.quote: This leud and dishonest Generation, which delighteth to deceive and cheat, had rather have a great then a good report
observations.note: This group prefers a great name to a good one.

observations.quote: it is truly praise-worthy to displease and vex these Cheaters that are for ever banished the society of all true Philosophers
observations.note: Displeasing them is praiseworthy; they are shut out of the company of true Philosophers.

observations.quote: as ignorant and unworthy of the mysteries of God, and the secrets of Nature
observations.note: The Cheaters are called ignorant and unworthy of the mysteries of God and the secrets of Nature.

observations.quote: the most laudable and honourable name of true and noble Alchymistry, hath been unworthily made infamous and odious
observations.note: True and noble Alchymistry is named as honourable and distinct from what the cheaters practise; he blames them for its ill repute.

observations.quote: among learned men, who yet have judged of others knowledge by their own ignorance
observations.note: Learned men too have held Alchymistry in ill repute, judging by their own ignorance.

observations.quote: that Spagyricall or Divinely-distinguishing Sanctuary
observations.note: The text sets 'Divinely-distinguishing' beside 'Spagyricall' as its other name; compare OPEN.7, Spagyriks as those who discern true from false.

observations.quote: what can make a man more renowned then to be dispraised of those most wretched Juglers and effeminate Yonkers
observations.note: Blame from such men is an honour, and their praise is oftentimes to be suspected.

observations.quote: These seek the commendation of ingenuity from the theft and calumny of their benefactors
observations.note: The margin says these men seek a name by stealing from and slandering those who helped them.

observations.quote: These are not the vices of the Art, but of men abusing the Art
observations.note: The margin lays the vices to men who abuse the Art, not to the Art; agrees with OPEN.7.

voices.quote: all the ancient Philosophers, by the example of Actaeon, have strictly forbidden
voices.basis: A rule reported with 'have strictly forbidden', under ALTHOUGH; the author sets himself against it with 'Notwithstanding'.

voices.quote: our Heavenly Father who is that Sun
